analysis.one_liner: Requires public companies to disclose their political spending, including money routed through trade associations and tax-exempt groups.
analysis.headline: The House Financial Services Committee approved the bill 28-23 on a party-line vote, but it never received a House floor vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend securities law to require every public company to file quarterly reports listing its political spending — the amount, the date, and the candidate supported or opposed — and to name any trade association or tax-exempt group receiving company dues that could be spent on politics. It would also require an annual summary of all political expenditures over $10,000 plus planned spending for the coming year, posted publicly in a searchable SEC database. The company's own shareholders and the general public could see, for the first time in one place, how corporate executives spend company money to influence elections.
analysis.who_benefits: Shareholders, who own the companies whose executives make the political spending decisions, and the general public, who would gain a searchable public record of corporate election spending — including spending routed anonymously through trade associations and 501(c) groups.

how_it_helps.text: Public companies must file quarterly reports listing each political expenditure, its amount and date, and the name, office, and party of any candidate it supported or opposed, and the SEC must make those reports publicly available in a searchable, sortable, downloadable database.

The disclosure reaches past direct giving: companies must name any trade association or 501(c) tax-exempt organization that receives dues or payments that are or could reasonably be used for political activity — the channels most often used to hide the original corporate funder.
Annual reports must summarize every political expenditure over $10,000 in the prior year and describe planned political spending for the coming year.
The SEC must assess issuer compliance each year and report to Congress, and the Government Accountability Office must periodically evaluate the SEC's oversight of the new requirements.

analysis.who_pays: Public companies that spend money on politics, and the trade associations and 501(c) groups they fund, would bear compliance costs and lose the ability to influence elections without anyone tracing the money back to them.
analysis.who_pays_short: Politically active public companies and trade groups

drawbacks.text: The rule reaches dues paid to trade associations that are merely 'reasonably anticipated' to fund politics. Dues are fungible — once money enters a trade association's general fund it is hard to trace — so the reported linkage between a company's dues and actual political spending may be imprecise, and companies may respond by cutting off association membership to avoid the reporting, reducing support for broad industry groups that also serve ordinary functions.

Public companies would bear recurring compliance costs to compile, verify, and report this spending every quarter, and business groups argue the disclosure burdens companies' participation in trade associations and civic activity rather than restricting any wrongdoing.

The bill only requires disclosure; it does not limit, cap, or ban any political spending, and it expressly excludes direct lobbying by registered lobbyists and corporate PAC contributions, which are already disclosed elsewhere.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real and structural: company money used to influence elections would become traceable to its corporate source, giving both shareholders and voters the information the bill's findings say they have historically lacked. The costs are limited to reporting burdens on affected companies, and the design is imperfect where money passes through trade association general funds, where attribution is necessarily an estimate. On balance the bill changes who has information — moving it from company executives alone to shareholders and the public — at a modest, well-defined cost.

outcome.mechanism: It cleared the House Financial Services Committee on a party-line 28-23 vote in April 2021, was reported to the House and placed on the House calendar in June 2021, and then sat there without a floor vote until the Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Rep. Bill Foster introduced the bill on February 18, 2021, and it was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services.
The committee held markup sessions on April 20-21, 2021, and ordered the bill reported as amended by a vote of 28-23.
The committee reported the amended bill on June 8, 2021 (H. Rept. 117-53) and it was placed on the Union Calendar, Calendar No. 36, meaning it was eligible for House floor consideration.
No further House action followed: the bill never received a floor vote, and the Congress ended on January 3, 2023 with the bill still on the calendar.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Public companies that spend on politics and the trade associations and tax-exempt groups they fund are better off, because corporate political spending remains undisclosed and untraceable. Shareholders and the public gain nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Corporate political spenders and dark-money groups

for.name: Rep. Bill Foster
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill in February 2021 and shepherded it through committee markup, where it was amended and reported in June 2021.

for.name: House Financial Services Committee Democrats
for.what_they_did: Voted 28-23 at the April 2021 markup to order the bill reported as amended, sending it to the House floor calendar.

for.name: 11 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republican signed on.

against.name: House Democratic leadership
against.role: House majority leadership in the 117th Congress
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a House floor vote after it was reported and placed on the Union Calendar in June 2021; it sat there until the Congress ended.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee Republicans
against.what_they_did: Provided the 23 no votes against ordering the bill reported at the April 2021 markup.

against.name: Business and trade-association lobbies
against.role: Opponents of corporate political-spending disclosure requirements
against.what_they_did: Publicly opposed disclosure mandates of this kind, arguing they burden companies' participation in trade associations and political activity.

sides.party_line_note: Every step split by party: all 11 cosponsors were Democrats, and the 28-23 committee vote to report the bill ran along party lines.

industries.industry: Publicly traded corporations that spend on politics
industries.note: These companies would have to itemize their political spending publicly every quarter, ending the ability of corporate executives to fund candidates and causes without shareholders or the public knowing. That anonymity is valuable to the companies and costs voters information about who is financing campaigns.

The bill would force companies to name any association or tax-exempt group receiving dues that could be used for politics, weakening their role as anonymous conduits between corporate funders and election spending — the mechanism popularly called dark money.

industries.industry: Asset managers and shareholder advocacy groups
industries.note: Large institutional investors and shareholder groups would get standardized, searchable data to hold company boards accountable for political spending with shareholder money.
